passage:
At the kindergarten lunch table, five-year-old Jatin opens his tiffin and, without a word, tears his paratha in half for his cousin Siddharth, who forgot his box. Ten minutes later they are tugging the same green crayon.
'Mine!'
'I had it first!'
It snaps, both howl, and Rekha Ma'am kneels between them. Before she can speak, Jatin hands over the longer piece, Siddharth gives him a sticker, and they go back to colouring one shared page. A classmate, hugging her own box, asks, 'Don't you want your own paper?' Jatin just looks puzzled.

qa.q: What did Jatin share with Siddharth at lunch?
qa.a: Half of his paratha.

qa.q: Why did Jatin look puzzled when the classmate asked about his own paper, and what was he feeling?
qa.a: He felt comfortable and happy sharing; with his cousin, one page for two seems normal, so wanting separate paper made no sense to him.

qa.q: What could Rekha Ma'am learn from how the boys made up?
qa.a: She could let them try to fix small quarrels themselves first and notice the quick repair, while staying close in case it does not settle.

qa.q: How might the classmate with her own box see the cousins' sharing?
qa.a: She may find it surprising or odd, since she keeps her own things, and might even wish for such an easy partner.

grounding: Shows a young child raised among cousins who shares food and things without being told, fights and makes up fast, and has no need yet for his own space.

passage:
From my balcony next door I watch Kavitha, five, and her four cousins sleep in one heap on a single mattress on their terrace on summer nights. Yesterday a mango came up. Kavitha bit it and passed it along without anyone asking; the smallest got the seed to suck. Later I heard a squabble over who got the spot by the wall, tears and a shove, and five minutes after, all of them giggling under one sheet. My daughter asked me why Kavitha doesn't have her own room. I didn't know. Kavitha never seems to want one.
Sangeeta

qa.q: Where do Kavitha and her cousins sleep on summer nights?
qa.a: On a single mattress on their terrace.

qa.q: What does Kavitha passing the mango along suggest she feels?
qa.a: It suggests she feels happy and at ease sharing, as if belonging with her cousins is simply normal, though Sangeeta can only guess from outside.

qa.q: What could Sangeeta tell the daughter who asked about Kavitha's room?
qa.a: That families live in different ways: Kavitha shares a lot and seems to enjoy it, and having your own room is fine too.

qa.q: Why might Sangeeta's daughter find Kavitha's life puzzling?
qa.a: The daughter probably has a separate room and things, so sharing a bed and a mango with many cousins looks strange.

grounding: Illustrates a young child among cousins who shares bed and food unasked, fights and makes up quickly, and does not seem to miss privacy, as seen by a neighbour.

passage:
Dadi's notebook, Sunday.

Five grandchildren slept in the big room again last night. Jasleen, five, gave her pillow to Darshan without anyone asking, then squeezed onto the corner of his mattress.

At breakfast the two fought over the last paratha. Tears, a push, and a loud "You're not my cousin anymore!"

Ten minutes later I found them on the stairs, splitting it and taking turns with the pickle.

What I did: nothing, only watched. Then I kneaded extra dough so tomorrow there will be two last parathas.

qa.q: What did Jasleen give Darshan?
qa.a: Jasleen gave her pillow to Darshan without anyone asking.

qa.q: What was Jasleen feeling when she shouted 'You're not my cousin anymore'?
qa.a: Jasleen felt angry and cheated over the last paratha, though the feeling passed within minutes.

qa.q: Which choice by Dadi worked, and why?
qa.a: Watching without stepping in let the cousins make up on their own, and extra dough for tomorrow gently heads off the next fight.

qa.q: How does Darshan experience sharing with Jasleen?
qa.a: For Darshan it is ordinary: he takes the pillow, fights, then splits the paratha on the stairs as if nothing broke.

grounding: Shows cousins in a joint home who share beds and food without being asked, and fight and make up quickly.

passage:
At Nanu's farmhouse near Nashik, the cousins ate mangoes on the back step. Sabina, five, took two big bites of hers, then held it out to Tejas without a word. Juice ran down to his elbow.

After lunch they fought over the tyre swing. Tejas shoved; Sabina yelled and stamped off behind the cowshed.

By teatime she was back, squashed on the swing beside him, the two of them counting to ten for each other's turn. Nobody had told them to make up.

qa.q: Where did Sabina stamp off to?
qa.a: Sabina stamped off behind the cowshed.

qa.q: How can you tell Sabina no longer felt angry about the swing?
qa.a: By teatime she was back and happy, squashed on the swing beside Tejas, taking turns, with no one telling them to make up.

qa.q: What could the grown-ups do next time the cousins fight?
qa.a: Give them a little time and space, as happened here, and step in only if someone could get hurt.

qa.q: How might Tejas feel when Sabina holds out her mango?
qa.a: Tejas probably feels pleased and included; sharing is simply normal among these cousins.

grounding: Illustrates a child among cousins sharing food unprompted and falling out and making up quickly.

passage:
In Grandma Ada's house in Enugu, six cousins shared one bedroom and one bathroom. When Aunty Chioma brought Amara a new box of crayons, Amara, five, tipped it straight onto the mat. "Everybody pick!"

Alejandro, visiting from Madrid, grabbed the green one and wouldn't give it back. Amara pulled; the crayon snapped. Both of them cried.

Then Amara laughed. "Now there's two greens!" She handed him half, and they drew one long green snake across the same page.

qa.q: What did Amara say when she tipped out the crayons?
qa.a: Amara said, "Everybody pick!"

qa.q: Why did Amara laugh after the crayon snapped?
qa.a: She went from upset to amused, seeing that a broken crayon meant two greens to share.

qa.q: How could an adult build on what Amara did?
qa.a: Praise her idea of sharing the halves and let the cousins keep drawing together, rather than rushing to buy a second box.

qa.q: What might the busy house feel like for Alejandro?
qa.a: Alejandro, visiting from Madrid, may be surprised that everything is shared, but the joint green snake shows he is being pulled right in.

grounding: Shows a child among cousins sharing a new gift without being asked and making up within moments after a fight.

passage: At the community centre's summer camp, Omkar, five, and his cousin Preeti sat together at lunch. Omkar broke his paratha and put half on Preeti's plate without a word. She gave him her banana. Then they both grabbed the red crayon. "Mine!" "No, mine!" Preeti pushed; Omkar cried. The teacher waited. Two minutes later, Omkar held out the crayon. "You do the sun, I do the car." Preeti nodded. By afternoon nap, they lay on one mat, feet touching.

qa.q: What did Omkar put on Preeti's plate?
qa.a: Half of his paratha.

qa.q: How did Omkar feel when he held out the crayon?
qa.a: He seemed ready to make up, no longer upset, wanting to play together again.

qa.q: Why did the teacher's choice to wait work well?
qa.a: It let the cousins fight and make up on their own, which they do quickly.

qa.q: What is it like for Preeti to share everything with Omkar?
qa.a: It probably feels natural and safe; sharing food and a mat is just normal for her.

grounding: It illustrates a child among cousins who shares without being asked, fights and makes up quickly.
